{{short description|Mathematical property}}
In [[mathematics]], '''finiteness properties''' of a [[Group (mathematics)|group]] are a collection of properties that allow the use of various [[Algebra|algebraic]] and [[Topology|topological]] tools, for example [[group cohomology]], to study the group. It is mostly of interest for the study of infinite groups. 

Special cases of groups with finiteness properties are [[finitely generated group|finitely generated]] and [[finitely presented group|finitely presented]] groups. 

== Topological finiteness properties ==

Given an [[integer]] ''n'' ≥ 1, a group <math>\Gamma</math> is said to be ''of type'' ''F''<sub>''n''</sub> if there exists an [[Aspherical space|aspherical CW-complex]] whose [[fundamental group]] is [[Group isomorphism|isomorphic]] to <math>\Gamma</math> (a [[classifying space]] for <math>\Gamma</math>) and whose [[n-skeleton|''n''-skeleton]] is finite. A group is said to be of type ''F''<sub>∞</sub> if it is of type ''F''<sub>''n''</sub> for every ''n''. It is of type ''F'' if there exists a finite aspherical CW-complex of which it is the fundamental group.

For small values of ''n'' these conditions have more classical interpretations: 
* a group is of type ''F''<sub>1</sub> if and only if it is [[Finitely generated group|finitely generated]] (the rose with petals indexed by a finite generating family is the 1-skeleton of a classifying space, the [[Cayley graph]] of the group for this generating family is the 1-skeleton of its universal cover);

* a group is of type ''F''<sub>2</sub> if and only if it is [[Presentation_of_a_group#Finitely_presented_groups|finitely presented]] (the [[presentation complex]], i.e. the rose with petals indexed by a finite generating set and 2-cells corresponding to each relation, is the 2-skeleton of a classifying space, whose universal cover has the [[Cayley complex]] as its 2-skeleton).

It is known that for every ''n'' ≥ 1 there are groups of type ''F''<sub>''n''</sub> which are not of type ''F''<sub>''n''+1</sub>. Finite groups are of type ''F''<sub>∞</sub> but not of type ''F''. [[Thompson groups|Thompson's group]] <math>F</math> is an example of a torsion-free group which is of type ''F''<sub>∞</sub> but not of type ''F''.<ref>{{cite journal | first1=Kenneth | last1=Brown | first2 = Ross | last2 = Geoghegan | title=An infinite-dimensional torsion-free ''FP''<sub>∞</sub> group | journal=Inventiones Mathematicae | year=1984 | volume=77 | issue=2 | pages=367–381 | doi=10.1007/BF01388451 | mr=0752825| s2cid=121877111 }}</ref>

A reformulation of the ''F''<sub>''n''</sub> property is that a group has it if and only if it [[Group action (mathematics)|acts]] properly discontinuously, freely and cocompactly on a CW-complex whose [[homotopy group]]s <math>\pi_0, \ldots, \pi_{n-1}</math> vanish. Another finiteness property can be formulated by replacing homotopy with homology: a group is said to be of type ''FH''<sub>n</sub> if it acts as above on a CW-complex whose ''n'' first homology groups vanish.

== Algebraic finiteness properties ==

Let <math>\Gamma</math> be a group and <math>\mathbb Z\Gamma</math> its [[group ring]]. The group <math>\Gamma</math> is said to be of type FP<sub>''n''</sub> if there exists a [[Resolution (algebra)|resolution]] of the trivial <math>\mathbb Z\Gamma</math>-[[Module (mathematics)|module]] <math>\mathbb Z</math> such that the ''n'' first terms are finitely generated [[projective module|projective]] <math>\mathbb Z\Gamma</math>-modules.{{sfn|Brown|1982|p=197}} The types ''FP''<sub>∞</sub> and ''FP'' are defined in the obvious way. 

The same statement with projective modules replaced by [[free module]]s defines the classes ''FL''<sub>''n''</sub> for ''n'' ≥ 1, ''FL''<sub>∞</sub> and ''FL''. 

It is also possible to define classes ''FP''<sub>''n''</sub>(''R'') and ''FL''<sub>''n''</sub>(''R'') for any [[commutative ring]] ''R'', by replacing the group ring <math>\mathbb Z\Gamma</math> by <math>R\Gamma</math> in the definitions above. 

Either of the conditions ''F''<sub>n</sub> or ''FH''<sub>''n''</sub> imply ''FP''<sub>''n''</sub> and ''FL''<sub>''n''</sub> (over any commutative ring). A group is of type ''FP''<sub>1</sub> if and only if it is finitely generated,{{sfn|Brown|1982|p=197}} but for any ''n'' ≥ 2 there exists groups which are of type ''FP''<sub>''n''</sub> but not ''F''<sub>''n''</sub>.<ref>{{citation |author-link=Mladen Bestvina |first1=Mladen |last1=Bestvina |first2=Noel |last2=Brady |title=Morse theory and finiteness properties of groups |journal=[[Inventiones Mathematicae]] |volume=129 |issue=3 |pages=445–470 |year=1997 |doi=10.1007/s002220050168 |bibcode=1997InMat.129..445B |s2cid=120422255 }}</ref>

If a group is of type ''F''<sub>''2''</sub> and ''FP''<sub>''n''</sub>, then it is of type ''F''<sub>''n''</sub>.

== Group cohomology ==
{{Main | Group cohomology}}

If a group is of type ''FP''<sub>''n''</sub> then its cohomology groups <math>H^i(\Gamma)</math> are finitely generated for <math>0 \le i \le n</math>. If it is of type ''FP'' then it is of finite cohomological dimension. Thus finiteness properties play an important role in the cohomology theory of groups. 

== Examples ==

=== Finite groups ===

A finite cyclic group <math>G</math> acts freely on the unit sphere in <math>\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}</math>, preserving a CW-complex structure with finitely many cells in each dimension.{{sfn|Brown|1982|p=20}} Since this unit sphere is contractible, every finite cyclic group is of type F<sub>∞</sub>.  

The standard resolution {{sfn|Brown|1982|p=18}} for a group <math>G</math> gives rise to a contractible CW-complex with a free <math>G</math>-action in which the cells of dimension <math>n</math> correspond to <math>(n+1)</math>-tuples of elements of <math>G</math>.  This shows that every finite group is of type F<sub>∞</sub>.  

A [[Trivial group|non-trivial]] finite group is never of type ''F'' because it has infinite cohomological dimension. This also implies that a group with a non-trivial [[torsion subgroup]] is never of type ''F''.

=== Nilpotent groups ===

If <math>\Gamma</math> is a [[Torsion (algebra)|torsion-free]], finitely generated [[nilpotent group]] then it is of type F.{{sfn|Brown|1982|p=213}}

=== Geometric conditions for finiteness properties ===

Negatively curved groups ([[Hyperbolic group|hyperbolic]] or [[CAT(0)]] groups) are always of type ''F''<sub>∞</sub>.{{sfn|Bridson|Haefliger|1999|p=439, 468}} Such a group is of type ''F'' if and only if it is torsion-free. 

As an example, cocompact [[S-arithmetic group]]s in [[algebraic group]]s over [[number field]]s are of type F<sub>∞</sub>. The Borel&ndash;Serre compactification shows that this is also the case for non-cocompact arithmetic groups. 

Arithmetic groups over [[Algebraic function field|function field]]s have very different finiteness properties: if <math>\Gamma</math> is an arithmetic group in a simple algebraic group of [[Maximal torus|rank]] <math>r</math> over a global function field (such as <math>\mathbb F_q(t)</math>) then it is of type F<sub>r</sub> but not of type F<sub>r+1</sub>.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bux |first1=Kai-Uwe |last2=Köhl |first2=Ralf |last3=Witzel |first3=Stefan |title=Higher finiteness properties of reductive arithmetic groups in positive characteristic: The Rank Theorem |journal=Annals of Mathematics |date=2013 |volume=177 |pages=311–366 |doi=10.4007/annals.2013.177.1.6|arxiv=1102.0428 |s2cid=53991649 }}</ref>
